text_to_speech: something that drew me into superconductivity when i was an undergraduate student thinking myself about what to do when i was introduced to superconductivity and levitation in particular i thought this is magic if the wheel would not have been invented so far we would not need it anymore we can do it just by levitation there is a subtle difference between levitation and suspension perfect levitation requires ideal meisner state and is not possible to suspend superconductor under the ferromagnet suspension requires magnetic flux to penetrate the interior of superconductor and be pinned people who've seen floating magnets and floating trains can see that there is virtually no loss as the magnet moves across the superconductor this is readily understandable in terms of forces on the magnet because the magnet is usually moving in a uniform field so there's no force on it however if you look at it from the point of view of the superconductor you've got these pinned flux lines so one might ask why are these being pulled along with the magnet which is an interesting question the answer is that the flux lines can cut and join in free space this is something which is not easy in a superconductor but in free space in the right geometry the flux lines can cut and rejoin because the flux lines don't actually exist this is true in a uniform field it's only when you've got non-uniformities that changes and movement will cause you to have forces

youtube_description:
A series of lectures on superconductivity. Courtesy of Professor Bartek Glowaki of the University of Cambridge, who filmed, directed and edited the videos.
This particular talk is about levitation using the fact that magnetic flux lines are excluded from a superconductor, the Meissner effect.
http://www.msm.cam.ac.uk/ascg/lectures/
